text:
Six review rounds on walmart-mvp PR #59, and every real defect was a confident wrong answer rather than an error. A 302 read a live token as dead. curl writes %{http_code} even when it never connects and then exits non-zero, so a `|| printf '000'` fallback appended to the 000 curl had already written, producing 000000, which matched no case arm; the network branch was dead code. `rerun` passed --branch=main to every trigger, so pointing it at the production trigger built main's tip while the confirmation screen said the operator was moving production from release. A guarded gcloud call set the build status to empty and the verdict tested only for FAILURE, so 'we could not look' printed as 'nothing to do'. An unreadable pinned version was reported as an unpublished one. None of these crashed. The tool's failure mode was fluency about the wrong thing, and each wrong answer aimed the operator away from the actual fault.

Second, and the one that cost most. A claim I had 'fixed everywhere' survived in the PR description and in two GitHub comments, because I grepped scripts/ and docs/ three times, got 'none left', and the repo is not where all the surfaces are. git grep cannot reach a PR body, a review comment, or a Slack message.

Third. gh authenticates as the account holder. I published agent-written prose under the owner's name with nothing marking it, and their team read it as the owner speaking; the owner discovered it live and hand-patched a marker on before telling me. Recorded as mist-20260818-142501-91, juror verdict very-wrong.

The thread worth dreaming on: my verification instinct scopes itself to the artifact I am editing. The claim's other homes, the identity the command posts under, the branch a flag defaults to, the case arm that can never match. Every one of these lived one step outside the thing I had open. Worth asking whether the fix is a habit of enumerating surfaces and identities before declaring a change complete, rather than a wider grep.
